In contrast, human head and neck tumors are characterized by dense extracellular matrix remodeling, enrichment of CAFs, aberrant vascular architecture, and elevated interstitial pressure, which significantly impede drug penetration and intratumoral distribution. 269 , 270 Furthermore, CAF-mediated extracellular matrix deposition and cytokine signaling promote immune evasion and therapeutic resistance, resulting in a more restrictive TME than that observed in most murine models. 271 Therefore, future studies should prioritize the development of more physiologically relevant models that more accurately recapitulate human tumor biology, including advanced in vitro three-dimensional culture systems and organ-on-a-chip technologies that capture the structural and functional complexity of human tissues and the TME. 272 Such advances will enable more accurate preclinical evaluation of NP-based therapies in HNCs and improve the predictive value for clinical translation.

sections.section: Heterogeneity Of The Epr Effect In Human Tumors
sections.text: The EPR effect has long been regarded as a cornerstone of passive drug delivery and is widely exploited in nanomedicine-based PDT and PTT. 273 In murine xenograft models, rapidly growing tumors typically exhibit highly permeable vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage, conditions that facilitate the accumulation of NPs. 274 However, an increasing body of clinical evidence indicates that EPR-mediated drug delivery in human tumors is highly heterogeneous. 275 In HNCs, vascular permeability, stromal density, and perfusion vary substantially across tumor regions and disease stages. These variations result in highly uneven NPs deposition and, consequently, limit the uniform distribution of ROS or heat within tumors. 276 Moreover, the dense stromal architecture and fibrosis commonly observed in human HNSCC further restrict the penetration of NPs beyond perivascular regions. As a result, the accumulation of NPs predicted from small-animal models frequently overestimates the achievable intratumoral drug levels in patients. 277 Future research should focus on the development of nanoplatforms capable of both efficient tumor accumulation and deep tissue penetration to enhance the overall therapeutic efficacy of phototherapy.

HPV infection has emerged as an independent etiological factor in HNSCC. The strongest association has been observed in the oropharynx, where HPV16 represents the most prevalent genotype. 278 HPV-positive and HPV-negative HNSCC exhibit fundamentally distinct biological behaviors and should be regarded as separate disease entities rather than merely molecular subtypes. 279 HPV-negative HNSCC is primarily driven by carcinogen-induced DNA damage, leading to frequent mutations in tumor suppressor genes such as tumor protein p53 (TP53) and cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A). In addition, the composition of immune infiltration differs markedly between HPV-positive and HPV-negative tumors. 280 Compared with HPV-negative HNSCC, HPV-positive tumors are characterized by a higher density of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. 281 Consequently, HPV-positive HNSCC displays distinct clinical and histopathological features, unique epidemiological patterns, and generally more favorable prognosis. From the perspective of phototherapy, these biological differences are of critical importance. HPV-positive tumors may be more susceptible to immune amplification following ICD, whereas HPV-negative tumors are more likely to be constrained by stromal barriers, hypoxia, and immune exclusion, thereby limiting therapeutic efficacy. 282

To enhance therapeutic efficacy, an increasing number of nanomedicine platforms incorporate multiple functional components, including targeting ligands, imaging probes, oxygen-generating catalytic modules, and immunomodulators. 283 However, the structural and functional complexity associated with synthesizing such multifunctional NPs and developing light-based systems leads to substantial increases in the cost of production. 284 Although these sophisticated designs demonstrate impressive performance in experimental settings, they also markedly complicate large-scale manufacturing and quality control. During scale-up, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency in critical parameters (eg, particle size distribution, surface chemistry, drug loading efficiency, and photophysical responsiveness) remains a major challenge 285 These manufacturing constraints hinder compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards and may delay regulatory approval processes. Furthermore, nanomedicine-based phototherapeutic systems are often classified as combination products that integrate drugs with medical devices (eg, laser systems or optical delivery platforms), thereby adding further complexity to regulatory evaluation and clinical trial design 286 Establishing standardized manufacturing workflows and scalable purification strategies is essential for broad clinical implementation. In parallel, economic considerations critically influence translational feasibility, as cost-effective and large-scale production is indispensable for global clinical adoption, particularly in resource-limited settings. 287 Addressing these manufacturing and regulatory bottlenecks is pivotal for advancing the widespread clinical translation and commercialization of NP-based targeted phototherapy.

Ensuring the biosafety of nanomedicine platforms is critical to minimizing unintended toxicities and enabling their clinical translation. Inorganic nanomaterials, such as AuNPs and carbon-based systems, are inherently non-biodegradable. This characteristic leads to potential long-term accumulation in organs such as the liver and spleen and raises concerns regarding chronic toxicity. 288 Although polymeric materials, including polypyrrole and PDA, are generally considered biocompatible and biodegradable, their long-term in vivo fate and potential cumulative toxicity require careful and systematic evaluation. 289 Additionally, it has been shown that biomimetic strategies (eg, cell membrane functionalization) enhance the accumulation of such materials in tumors Nevertheless, the intrinsic immunogenicity of biological coatings (eg, derived from cell membranes or viral proteins) may trigger unpredictable immune recognition and clearance mechanisms 290 These biosafety concerns further complicate the clinical application of nanomedicine-based phototherapy, as the long-term metabolic behavior, biodistribution, and stability of these materials must be comprehensively characterized. Future studies should prioritize rigorous pharmacokinetic profiling and nanotoxicological assessments to ensure the safety of these materials and facilitate regulatory approval.

The integration of phototherapy with advanced ultrasound technologies represents a promising direction for targeted treatment of HNCs. The NIR-II window offers reduced attenuation, minimal tissue autofluorescence, and low phototoxicity, thereby enabling deeper tissue penetration and improved spatial resolution for imaging. 291 Unlike light, ultrasound can penetrate tissues to depths of up to ~10 cm, effectively overcoming the limited penetration associated with PTT and minimizing collateral damage to surrounding healthy tissues. In addition, Ultrasound can promote NP extravasation via acoustic cavitation and facilitate localized drug release, thus enabling greater tissue penetration. 292 Consequently, photoacoustic imaging-guided PTT enables real-time monitoring of photothermal distribution and facilitates adaptive treatment modulation, thus enhancing therapeutic precision and safety. 257 , 293 These advances pave the way for highly personalized and minimally invasive PTT interventions in HNCs.

sections.section: Synergistic Effects Of Phototherapy And Immunotherapy
sections.text: Immunotherapy in HNCs is frequently constrained by a profoundly immunosuppressive TME, which is characterized by the upregulation of chemokines such as C-C motif chemokine ligand 22 (CCL22) and CCL28, accumulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells, polarization of macrophages and neutrophils toward protumorigenic phenotypes, and suppression of T cell and natural killer cell activity. 294 , 295 Within this context, CAFs constitute a dominant stromal cell population that actively supports tumor progression. CAFs promote immune evasion by secreting immunosuppressive cytokines, including transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), IL-10, and IL-6, as well as by expressing immune checkpoint ligands such as PD-L1 and PD-L2. Moreover, CAFs generate a dense extracellular matrix rich in collagen, fibronectin, and proteoglycans (eg, hyaluronan and versican), forming a physical barrier that limits immune cell infiltration and impedes the penetration of phototherapeutic agents 296 In addition, CAF-driven signaling networks facilitate the recruitment and activation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and tumor-associated macrophages, which secrete cytokines (eg, IL-6, IL-10) and granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), thereby reinforcing an immunosuppressive TME and promoting macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype 297 , 298 Of note, PD-L1 (a key immune checkpoint molecule) mediates immune escape by binding to PD-1 on lymphocytes and suppressing T cell activation. Importantly, PD-L1 expression exhibits pronounced spatial heterogeneity across tumor cells, stromal components, and infiltrating immune cells. 299 This characteristic complicates its use as a predictive biomarker and reflects the adaptive nature of immune evasion within the TME. As discussed above, the ability of PDT and PTT to induce ICD positions them as powerful immunomodulatory partners capable of converting immunologically “cold” tumors into “hot” tumors. This process enhances the responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade and other immunotherapies. Accordingly, the combination of PDT/PTT with immune checkpoint inhibitors, cancer vaccines, or adoptive T cell therapies holds substantial promise for eliciting durable systemic antitumor responses against both primary and metastatic lesions. 256 , 300 Such combinations may ultimately transform phototherapy from a local modality into a systemic therapeutic strategy.

sections.section: Precision Phototherapy Based On Tumor Molecular Stratification
sections.text: HNCs exhibit marked heterogeneity in genetic composition, biomarker expression, oxygenation status, and therapeutic response; hence, standardized treatment regimens often fail to meet the needs of individual patients. 301 Accordingly, the transition toward personalized and precision medicine is critical for advancing nanomedicine-based targeted phototherapy. Integrative analysis of high-throughput multi-omics data—including genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics—enables the stratification of patients who are more likely to benefit from PDT. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning approaches can leverage large-scale clinical and molecular datasets, encompassing genetic profiles, tumor characteristics, and treatment histories, to predict optimal phototherapy strategies tailored to specific molecular subtypes. 302 Such data-driven precision approaches hold considerable promise for improving therapeutic outcomes and advancing individualized treatment paradigms in HNCs.

sections.section: Ai-Assisted Design Of Nps For Phototherapy
sections.text: AI has emerged as a transformative tool with the potential to rapidly and accurately design novel photosensitizer candidates with low toxicity and high photodynamic activity, based on existing datasets of well-characterized and biocompatible molecules. 303 , 304 Such data-driven approaches enable the efficient identification of optimized molecular structures, thereby facilitating the development of safer and more effective targeted phototherapies for HNCs. These intelligent systems support high-throughput virtual screening, reduce material waste, and accelerate the discovery of high-performance nanomaterials. 305 The integration of AI with nanotechnology offers significant opportunities for precision design, enhanced efficiency, and accelerated clinical translation, emphasizing the key role of this interdisciplinary approach in the future of biomedical nanotechnology.

The successful clinical translation of nanomedicine-based phototherapy requires close interdisciplinary collaboration and the integration of expertise from precision medicine, nanotechnology, optical physics, AI, and oncology. 306 The convergence of these disciplines has driven the development of multifunctional nanoplatforms that integrate therapeutic efficacy with diagnostic precision. By fostering interdisciplinary integration, aligning technological innovation with clinical needs, and establishing standardized evaluation frameworks, targeted phototherapy for HNCs can be further optimized to achieve improved efficacy, enhanced safety, and broader clinical applicability.

Although nanomedicine-based phototherapy remains at an early stage of clinical translation, the field is nonetheless undergoing rapid advances at both the preclinical and technological levels. With the rapid advancement of nanotechnology, nanomedicine-based targeted phototherapy has emerged as a transformative strategy for the treatment of HNCs. This treatment modality leverages the unique physicochemical properties of nanomaterials to significantly enhance the efficacy and specificity of PDT and PTT. In the present review, we summarized recent progress in the development of next-generation photosensitizers, design of multifunctional nanocarriers, and integration of phototherapy with both conventional and emerging therapeutic modalities for the treatment of HNCs. Despite these impressive scientific advances, the clinical translation of targeted phototherapy remains cautious and is limited by major challenges. A primary concern lies in the potential toxicity associated with nanomedicine platforms. 307 Although multifunctional nanoplatforms demonstrate robust performance in preclinical studies, their translation into clinical practice is hindered by regulatory complexity and incomplete safety evaluation. Currently, the biocompatibility and safety profiles of numerous emerging and hybrid nanomaterials remain insufficiently characterized, with a lack of standardized validation for their absorption, distribution, pharmacokinetics, and long-term toxicity. Moreover, complex synthesis processes, challenges in manufacturing scalability, and stringent regulatory requirements further complicate reproducibility and clinical approval. These parameters constitute major bottlenecks for the transition from laboratory-scale synthesis to industrial-scale production. Future efforts should prioritize the harmonization of nanotoxicological assessment, establishment of standardized manufacturing workflows, and development of scalable purification strategies to enable widespread clinical implementation. In parallel, large-scale and cost-effective production is essential for global clinical adoption. Furthermore, innovations in green synthesis and economically sustainable manufacturing processes may play a pivotal role in ensuring accessibility and affordability across diverse healthcare settings. AI also represents a transformative tool for the rational design of nanoplatforms. By leveraging datasets of well-characterized photosensitizer and photothermal agent molecules, AI-driven approaches can optimize key parameters such as optical absorption, quantum yield, and biodistribution, thereby accelerating the development of safer and more effective next-generation phototherapeutic systems for HNCs. 308 Another critical challenge lies in the pronounced variability of the EPR effect across patients, tumor types, and different temporal stages of the same tumor. Such heterogeneity limits the predictability and efficiency of NP delivery. In particular, the penetration of NPs into large, poorly perfused, and deep-seated pharyngeal tumors remains inadequate, resulting in the uneven distribution of ROS or heat within the tumor mass. Recent advances in organic–inorganic hybrid nanostructures and biomimetic cell membrane-functionalized platforms have demonstrated improved translational potential by achieving a balance between optical performance and biocompatibility. The development of intelligent multifunctional nanoplatforms responsive to NIR-II light, ultrasound, or X-ray irradiation may further expand the applicability and safety of phototherapy for deep-seated head and neck tumors. 309 Most current preclinical studies rely heavily on in vitro two-dimensional cell culture systems and murine subcutaneous tumor models, which fail to recapitulate the physicochemical complexity of the human TME. Moreover, patient-derived xenograft models established in immunodeficient mice lack a functional tumor immune microenvironment, thereby limiting their ability to accurately reproduce human tumor immunobiology. As a result, these models provide only partial insight into therapeutic responses and may overestimate translational efficacy. Future research should prioritize the development of more physiologically relevant models, including advanced three-dimensional in vitro systems and organ-on-a-chip technologies capable of capturing the structural and functional characteristics of human tissues and the TME. 310 Such innovations may enable more accurate preclinical evaluation of NP-based phototherapy and improve the predictive power for clinical translation in human tumors. In addition, the pronounced heterogeneity of HNCs poses a significant challenge to the therapeutic efficacy of photoactivated nanoplatforms. Variations in genetic alterations, molecular phenotypes, and features of the TME can lead to divergent treatment responses, thereby complicating the optimization of phototherapy strategies. AI and machine learning approaches offer powerful tools for processing and learning from large-scale patient datasets. By integrating high-throughput multi-omics data (eg, genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics) these technologies can facilitate the identification of novel predictive biomarkers associated with phototherapy responsiveness 311 Such advances may enable the stratification of patients most likely to benefit from phototherapy and pave the way for precision phototherapeutic strategies based on tumor molecular profiling. Nanomedicine-based targeted phototherapy represents a rapidly advancing field of research in the treatment of HNCs, particularly when synergistically integrated with advances in optical physics. Such convergence holds the potential to transform phototherapy from a promising adjunctive modality into an established and clinically recognized therapeutic strategy. Although the transition from laboratory research to clinical application is likely to be gradual and challenged by substantial obstacles, continued interdisciplinary innovation and translational efforts are expected to drive this evolution. Ultimately, precision and individualized phototherapy enabled by nanomedicine may redefine the therapeutic landscape for HNCs.
